passages.section: La-JEPA: Compact Robot Policies with Latent World Modeling
passages.location: La-JEPA: Compact Robot Policies with Latent World Modeling
passages.text: World-action models commonly adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on pretrained vision-language backbones; both tie policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. While the knowledge accumulated through large-scale pretraining is certainly useful, it remains unclear how much generation-oriented architectural choices affect control performance, and whether the trade-off required to access this pretraining is worth it. In this work, we introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA) , a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder, so that its architecture and capacity can be chosen for control. Following Fast-WAM, La-JEPA learns to predict future features jointly with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art performance in clean and randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes and on LIBERO-Plus with correct instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competing policies. It runs substantially faster than Fast-WAM at comparable performance and outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0 without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, including contact-heavy pushing and long-horizon multistep manipulation, its average success is comparable to π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , outperforming non-embodied-pretrained baselines. Through a design study of the choices behind La-JEPA, we show that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction choices significantly impact the policy even when future prediction is skipped at inference. We also correct the LIBERO-Plus instructions, as the officially released evaluator corrupts them for most variants, and re-evaluate several strong open baselines. These results establish a compact, efficient foundation for JEPA-based world-action modeling: without a generative pretrained policy backbone, La-JEPA is better and faster than far larger policies built on video and language generation models, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed specifically for control rather than inherited from generation.

World-action models increasingly adapt pretrained video-generation transformers to robot control, inheriting useful visual and temporal priors along with the representation space, tokenization, and architecture of a model built for video synthesis ( Yuan et al., 2026b ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) . Vision-language-action policies take a similar route using language-generation transformers aligned with visual inputs ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . The success of these two types of architectures raises two practical questions: must robot policies necessarily inherit the architecture of a generative backbone to be competitive, and can a compact world-action transformer trained from scratch actually reach the performance of these policies?

Most world-action models (WAMs) are VAE-based because they build on pretrained video generators, yet better-suited latent spaces are available. Video VAEs retain accurate information but spend much of their capacity on pixel-level fidelity that control does not require. JEPA representations, in contrast, are developed and evaluated for downstream tasks such as video understanding, depth estimation, and segmentation, which are closer to the needs of embodied agents ( Assran et al., 2025 ; Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) . Previous work aligns VLMs or video-generation models to the JEPA space ( Lin et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) or learns a JEPA-style latent space jointly with the policy ( Vujinovic & Kovacevic, 2025 ) ; to our knowledge, no prior work trains a compact world-action policy from scratch in a pretrained JEPA feature space.

We introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA) , a world-action model that learns future-feature prediction and action generation directly in the dense spatial and temporal feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 video encoder ( Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) . Its World DiT and Action DiT are initialized from scratch, allowing their architecture and capacity to be chosen independently of the visual encoder. Following Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026b ; Ma et al., 2026 ) , actions attend to observed context but not to future tokens, so predictive supervision can shape the policy during training without the cost of generating the future at inference time.

Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves the strongest clean and randomized RoboTwin 2.0 results and the strongest LIBERO-Plus results with corrected instructions (Section 5.2 ), with about four times fewer deployed parameters than the next-best policies, while running up to 5 × \times faster than Fast-WAM, whose design we follow (Figure 1 , Tables 1 and 2 ). With the released instructions, it is second only to NowWAM, which is insensitive to the corrupted text (Table 14 ). It also outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0 (Table 3 ). On real-robot tasks ranging from cube placement to contact-rich pushing and long-horizon manipulation, La-JEPA trained from scratch on the target demonstrations achieves the highest average success among the compared policies, comparable to the embodied-pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} (Table 5 ). Together, these results demonstrate leading benchmark performance, efficient inference, and competitive physical manipulation without requiring a generative backbone.

To understand which design choices enable this performance, we study the impact of the representation space, different targets for predictive supervision, and robustness mechanisms. We adopt a compact first approach, making the architecture viable even for a policy with 0.1B trainable parameters, before increasing policy capacity. Comparisons of JEPA features and VAE latents span both benchmarks and multiple model configurations, showing that JEPA features generally outperform VAE latents, with the clearest gains for out of distribution evaluations (Section 4.1 , Appendix A.1 ). Action-only controls separately confirm the benefit of WAM-style future prediction, and studies of temporal encoding, dropout, augmentation, and encoder adaptation complete the recipe. These analyses support the central contribution: a compact, effective world-action policy, together with evidence to guide its design. As a secondary contribution, we show that the released LIBERO-Plus evaluator appends perturbation parameters to most instructions, so that most variants apply two perturbations at once. This corruption affects policies to very different degrees, from no change to 19 points, and obscures the robustness study that the benchmark is designed for; we therefore re-evaluate the openly available baselines with corrected instructions under a single “clean” protocol that isolates each perturbation as intended (Section 5.2 ).

Vision-language-action (VLA) policies extend pretrained vision-language models with action outputs, predicting discretized action tokens ( Kim et al., 2024 ) or attaching a flow-matching action expert ( Black et al., 2024 ) , and broaden their training data to generalize further ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026a ) . All inherit the size and inference cost of a multi-billion-parameter vision-language backbone.

World-action models (WAMs) instead build on pretrained video or image generators whose representations drive action generation ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) , reaching the strongest previously reported LIBERO-Plus results among policies without embodied pretraining. Because generating future frames slows inference, recent WAMs predict the future only during training ( Yuan et al., 2026b ) and reduce the action expert to a single layer that reads keys and values cached from all layers of the video backbone ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . All retain the generator backbone in the deployed policy.

Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn representations by predicting the embeddings of masked inputs rather than reconstructing pixels ( Assran et al., 2023 ) . V-JEPA extends this objective to video ( Bardes et al., 2024 ) , V-JEPA 2 scales it ( Assran et al., 2025 ) , and V-JEPA 2.1 improves the dense features of V-JEPA 2 ( Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) , which makes it especially well suited to robotic policies. JEPA representations have since been used in robot policies: ACT-JEPA learns a JEPA-style latent space jointly with the policy ( Vujinovic & Kovacevic, 2025 ) , VLA-JEPA and JEPA-VLA bring V-JEPA targets or features into vision-language-action models ( Sun et al., 2026 ; Miao et al., 2026 ) , and JEPA-WAM and LeapBot-WA build world-action models on V-JEPA features ( Lin et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . These two world-action models are the closest to La-JEPA, but both initialize their predictors from pretrained vision-language or video generation models.

Policies that are competitive without inheriting either a VLM or video backbone are scarce. While Diffusion Policy ( Chi et al., 2023 ) , DP3 ( Ze et al., 2024 ) and ACT ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) exist, their performance is rarely close to VLAs and World Models. MINT predicts coarse-to-fine action tokens with a separately trained action tokenizer ( Huang et al., 2026 ) and reaches much better success rates, but remains below the strongest WAMs and VLAs. La-JEPA fits in this category as it trains its policy DiTs from scratch while adding WAM-style future prediction in a pretrained JEPA feature space.

La-JEPA learns action generation jointly with future-feature prediction in a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-L representation space, following the separation of training-time world modeling from inference-time action generation in Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026b ) and Faster-WAM ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . At decision time t t , the policy maps multi-camera observations o t o_{t} , proprioception s t s_{t} , and a language instruction ℓ \ell to an action chunk A = ( a t , … , a t + H − 1 ) A=(a_{t},\ldots,a_{t+H-1}) . This section describes the fixed architecture and training procedure (Figure 2 ); Section 4 examines the choices within it.

The pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-L encoder ( Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) processes each camera independently, producing observation features z ctx z_{\mathrm{ctx}} from the most recent frames, and future targets z fut z_{\mathrm{fut}} representing the 32 frames ahead. We normalize and spatially reduce these feature grids before projecting them into the World DiT’s embedding space. They are the model’s only visual input and prediction target, so the model gets no separate RGB pathway. Future predictions are matched to targets directly in V-JEPA space and require no pixel reconstruction.

A frozen FLAN-T5-large encoder ( Chung et al., 2022 ) embeds the instruction ℓ \ell , and learned projections map proprioception s t s_{t} to additional tokens; together they form the conditioning sequence z cond z_{\mathrm{cond}} , which both DiTs read through cross-attention.

The model is made of two diffusion transformers (DiTs) ( Peebles & Xie, 2022 ) : a World DiT over observation and future-feature tokens and an Action DiT over the action chunk. Both are initialized from scratch with separate attention projections and feed-forward layers, so pretrained knowledge enters only through the visual and language encoders. Rotary visual positional encodings ( Su et al., 2021 ) preserve spatial and temporal information. The two DiTs interact at every layer, where action queries read the World DiT’s observation keys and values alongside its own. The attention mask keeps future information out of the action pathway: observation tokens attend only to observations, future tokens to observations and futures, and action tokens to observations and actions. Actions therefore never access future features directly, yet predictive supervision still shapes the observation representations they read through the shared World DiT parameters during training.

We test the design choices behind Section 5 with the small (S) policy unless stated otherwise. We ask, in turn, whether to predict future features, in which feature space, how to encode motion (Section 4.1 ), and then how to make the policy robust to observation changes (Section 4.2 ). The studies use LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and clean-trained RoboTwin 2.0 ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Fei et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) ; in-distribution (IID) evaluation refers to LIBERO or clean RoboTwin scenes, and out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation to LIBERO-Plus or randomized scenes. Figure 3 reports each choice’s gain in success in percentage points (hereafter, points), grouped into blocks A to F. Each block has its own reference recipe, so comparisons hold within a block; Table 6 lists baselines and evaluation budgets, and Appendix A documents the protocols.

We first test whether predicting future features benefits the policy, comparing joint action and future-feature prediction with action-only training (Figure 3 A). Future prediction raises RoboTwin success by 7.0 points in clean and 3.7 in randomized scenes. On LIBERO-Plus, it improves success for each of three training seeds, by 2.1 points on average, with every paired comparison significant ( p < 0.01 p<0.01 , McNemar; Appendix A.1 ).

We next ask in which space prediction should be learned, comparing frozen V-JEPA 2.1 features with latents of the VAE of Wan2.2 ( Team Wan et al., 2025 ) , the video model underlying Fast-WAM, Faster-WAM, and LeapBot-WA (Figure 3 B). Each policy learns action and future-feature prediction with the normalization and projections suited to its representation, so the comparison evaluates each representation together with its interface to the policy. V-JEPA improves success in all four evaluations of this pair: by 15.9 points in clean and 16.0 in randomized RoboTwin scenes, and by 6.0 on LIBERO-Plus and 2.0 on LIBERO. In randomized scenes, the Wan2.2 policy collapses and succeeds in only 1.0% of episodes, close to the video-generator WAMs in Table 2 . In two additional RoboTwin comparisons (Appendix A.1 ), clean success is comparable in one and favors Wan2.2 in the other, whereas randomized success, reported for the second, again strongly favors V-JEPA. These results echo those of LDA-1B, which similarly reports a large gain from replacing VAE latents with DINO features ( Lyu et al., 2026 ) .

Unlike LDA-1B’s DINO, which only encodes images, V-JEPA 2.1 can process videos, which raises the question of how the observations and future targets should be encoded. We tested three configurations. Static encodings treat every frame as an image: the observation is the current frame, and eight future targets, spaced four frames apart up to 32 frames ahead, are encoded separately. Tube encoding instead processes two-frame clips aligned with the encoder’s tubelets, ending at the current frame for the observation and at each target frame for the futures; the observation clip thus gives the policy a motion cue without access to future observations. Tube-motion keeps the tube observation but jointly encodes the 16 future frames, spaced two frames apart, so each of the eight future feature grids attends over the whole predicted horizon (Figure 2 , right). Relative to static encoding on RoboTwin (Figure 3 C), tube encoding raises clean success by 1.1 points and randomized success by 3.6, and tube-motion preserves the randomized gain ( + 3.7 +3.7 ) while raising the clean gain to 3.4; the final recipe therefore uses tube-motion.

Before entering the World DiT, the encoded feature grids are reduced spatially, either by averaging neighboring features (mean pooling) or by concatenating them into one token (patch grouping). We initially used mean pooling for its simplicity, since it can be applied once to the precomputed features. On RoboTwin, patch grouping improved randomized success, so the final RoboTwin recipe uses it; LIBERO did not benefit from it (89.35% against 94.05% with mean pooling), so we kept mean pooling there (Appendix A.1 ).

To reduce reliance on any single view, we drop eligible cameras during training, always retaining at least one view and removing the dropped cameras’ future targets from the loss (Figure 3 D). This is the condition dropout used to train classifier-free guidance ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) , although we sample without guidance. Dropping only the wrist cameras raises randomized RoboTwin success by 7.1 points, while clean success remains essentially unchanged. LIBERO benefits from this too: by allowing either camera to be dropped, we raise LIBERO-Plus success by 10.2 points, with large gains under camera-viewpoint and sensor-noise perturbations (Table 8 ), while in-distribution success slightly improves.

Dropping the proprioceptive conditioning with probability 0.1 during training, with the configuration otherwise unchanged, raises RoboTwin success by 3.8 points in clean and 4.2 in randomized scenes (Figure 3 E). The final recipe therefore uses both camera and proprioception dropout.

Finally, we combine image augmentation of the observations with LoRA ( Hu et al., 2021 ) adaptation of the observation encoder; future targets are still computed from unmodified frames by the original encoder for training efficiency purposes (Appendix B ). Relative to a plain LIBERO policy (Figure 3 F), LoRA alone adds 1.4 points on LIBERO-Plus, augmentation alone 5.8, and both together 7.2, while in-distribution success remains unchanged. The combined recipe also improves RoboTwin, raising clean success by 5.7 points and randomized success by 16.0 (Appendix A.2 ).

These studies define the final recipe: joint action and future prediction in V-JEPA 2.1 tube-motion features, camera and proprioception dropout, and image augmentation with encoder LoRA. We train it at three sizes, S, B, and L (Table 9 ), which correspond to 0.10, 0.34, and 1.14 B trainable parameters respectively. Appendix B documents the remaining benchmark-specific settings.

We evaluate the final recipe against WAM and VLA policies that, like La-JEPA, use no embodied pretraining on robot data beyond the target demonstrations (Figure 1 , Tables 1 and 2 ), and against the closest latent world-action models (Table 3 ); we then compare computational cost and, on four physical tasks, real-robot success (Table 5 ). Both benchmarks test generalization beyond the training distribution. On RoboTwin, policies are trained on clean demonstrations only and evaluated in both clean scenes and randomized scenes, which add clutter, distractor objects, and new textures. On LIBERO, policies are trained on the four standard suites and evaluated both on them and on LIBERO-Plus, which perturbs them along seven axes such as camera viewpoint, lighting, and sensor noise. On RoboTwin, all three La-JEPA sizes outperform every baseline in both regimes, with the largest margin in randomized scenes (Table 2 ). On LIBERO-Plus, success increases with size. With the released instructions, L exceeds every baseline except NowWAM ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , which deploys four times more parameters; with corrected instructions (Section 5.2 ), all three sizes exceed or match every re-evaluated baseline, and L leads NowWAM by 1.8 points. On LIBERO, where most methods are close to saturation, all three sizes come within 0.6 points of the best baseline.

RoboTwin success, in contrast, does not monotonically increase with size. We did not vary the relative size of the Action DiT, which matches the World DiT at every size, and we hypothesize that a larger action expert more easily overfits the action distribution, which is far simpler than the distribution of future features, even when regularized by the world loss. Faster-WAM, whose single-layer action expert generalizes well on LIBERO-Plus ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , is consistent with this hypothesis.

The released LIBERO-Plus evaluator corrupts the instructions of 8,493 of its 10,030 variants by appending the perturbation’s parameters (Table 4 ); Flex- π \pi ( Yan et al., 2026a ) noted this issue but substitutes BDDL annotations that paraphrase the training instructions for most variants, so that the language remains perturbed. We therefore also evaluate all open policies with corrected in-distribution instructions (Appendix B ). The corruption affects video-generator-based WAMs most strongly, obscuring their true robustness to several perturbations: with corrected instructions, Fast-WAM gains 19.3 points, LeapBot-WA 8.1, and Cosmos Policy 4.1, whereas image-generator-based WAMs and VLM-based policies change by at most 1.4 points and La-JEPA gains 3.9 to 6.3. With corrected instructions, every La-JEPA size exceeds every re-evaluated policy without embodied pretraining (Table 1 ), and L leads NowWAM by 1.8 points with four times fewer deployed parameters; it also exceeds the embodied-pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and π \pi -JEPA-WAM (Table 14 ).

La-JEPA also outperforms the two closest JEPA-based world-action models on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, although both retain pretrained predictors (Table 3 ). LeapBot-WA, which also pretrains on robot data and deploys 10.4B parameters, falls below all three La-JEPA sizes on LIBERO-Plus with both the released and the corrected instructions (Table 14 in Appendix B ). JEPA-WAM, built on a pretrained Qwen2.5 model ( Qwen et al., 2024 ) , is exceeded on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus by all three La-JEPA sizes, S and B deploying fewer parameters. On RoboTwin, JEPA-WAM trains and evaluates on 20 of the 50 tasks, and on these tasks every La-JEPA size, trained on all 50, leads it by more than 15 points in clean and 9 points in randomized scenes. This subset is easier than the full benchmark, since per-task DP3 and ACT policies score about 20 points higher on it in clean scenes (Appendix B ); because it was chosen by JEPA-WAM and applies equally to both methods, we do not consider the comparison biased in our favor. Even when JEPA-WAM’s scores are extrapolated to all 50 tasks using this difficulty gap, every La-JEPA size remains ahead in both regimes. LDA-1B, pretrained on over 30k hours of human and robot data with a 4B vision-language model ( Lyu et al., 2026 ) , remains far below on both benchmarks ( Yan et al., 2026b ) .

La-JEPA updates 0.10 to 1.14 B parameters during training, far fewer than the video-generator and vision-language-action baselines (2.0 to 7.8 B; Tables 1 and 2 ) while showing lower replan latency at matched or better performance. We time complete policy calls, with ten denoising steps on one consumer GPU (Table 15 , Appendix C ). With optimized (compiled) builds, S and B run two to five times faster than Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM, and S with original-kernel CUDA graphs, which reproduce uncompiled actions bit-for-bit, remains 2.6 × \times faster than optimized Fast-WAM. Compiled builds do not significantly change closed-loop LIBERO success (Appendix C ), and the physical-robot policy runs compiled. Reducing inference to three denoising steps lowers latency further while keeping success within about one point (Appendix E.2 ), consistent with evidence that diffusion policies do not require many denoising steps ( Clémente et al., 2025 ) .

We train a La-JEPA B policy from scratch, with encoder LoRA but without image augmentation, on demonstrations of four Franka tabletop tasks (Figure 5 ; Appendix D ) and compare it with Fast-WAM, Faster-WAM, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and LingBot-VA ( Li et al., 2026 ) in Table 5 . We start with a simple cube placement as control, then test on fruit picking which requires lifting a lid, setting it down, and choosing the correct fruit; Push T tests contact-heavy interactions; and our dish task requires placing two plates from a rack onto the table, then a spoon on the gray plate and a fork on the pink plate in one uninterrupted rollout, with interchangeable utensil positions that require distinguishing the utensils.

La-JEPA achieves the highest average success among policies without embodied pretraining and is comparable to the embodied-pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , although its policy transformer is trained only on the target demonstrations. It is the most successful policy on Push T, whereas π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} leads on the long-horizon dish task. On successful trials, La-JEPA also completes every task faster than the other policies without embodied pretraining (Appendix D ), and faster than π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on fruit picking and Push T, though slower on the dish task. LingBot-VA rarely succeeds on Push T and dish manipulation and is several times slower than every other policy. LingBot-VA’s low success may reflect a need for more real-robot finetuning than the shared budget allowed (Appendix D ).

We aim to show the potential of compact world-action policies rather than to optimize them exhaustively: beyond the targeted design studies, we did not systematically search learning rates, weight decay, dropout rates, LoRA configurations, or the relative capacity of the World and Action DiTs. This lack of scale-specific tuning, together with limited target data, may contribute to the non-monotonic RoboTwin scaling; our experiments do not isolate these effects. We also recognize that many high-performing baselines have external supervision objectives and robot-specific architectures that we do not: while this work does outline the performance of a policy with a simple setup, we cannot be certain that our improvements would stack with other work’s policy upgrades.

Our policies learn from target demonstrations alone, so how La-JEPA scales with embodied pretraining remains open. Adapting the policy and its visual representation across embodiments and environments would also test whether data, rather than capacity, limits the larger models. We consider this the principal future direction of research that should come out of this paper. La-JEPA remains below the strongest embodied-pretrained methods on randomized RoboTwin scenes, and its real-robot average, although comparable to that of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , comes from four tasks on one robot setup and does not establish parity across broader manipulation demands. The richer supervision, synthetic data, and additional objectives used by some stronger baselines are natural extensions of La-JEPA that we have not tested.

We asked whether world-action policies must inherit the architecture of a generative backbone, and whether a compact transformer trained from scratch can compete with those that do. Trained in a pretrained JEPA feature space, La-JEPA reaches the strongest RoboTwin 2.0 clean and randomized results among policies without embodied pretraining, and the strongest LIBERO-Plus results once the benchmark’s corrupted instructions are corrected, while running up to 5 × \times faster than Fast-WAM. On four physical tasks, La-JEPA’s average success is comparable to that of the embodied-pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . Through our study, we empirically validate the benefits of the V-JEPA latent space for control tasks, provide some guidance on the benefits of different robustness design improvements and find that heavy generative models are not a requirement for high-performing learned policies.

In this work, we used generative AI tools to implement methods, including the optimization of the training and dataloading pipeline which was particularly heavy, evaluation, and data-preprocessing code; to reformat datasets into precomputed feature stores (always through verifiable scripts); and to help design the infrastructure that enabled the interpretation of our large amount of results. We did not use generative AI tools to generate synthetic data, develop theoretical models, formulate or prove mathematical claims, or translate text; these uses are not applicable to this work. Additionally, we used generative AI tools to edit parts of the paper, to write the code that generates figures and tables from recorded results, to search for and summarize related literature, and to format references. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work: code was tested and validated against recorded outputs, reported numbers were traced to their evaluation records, figures and tables are generated by code from the underlying data directly, never by the AI tool itself, and references were checked against their arXiv entries. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

This work uses public simulation benchmarks and robot demonstrations collected by the authors through teleoperation; it involves no human-subject studies and releases no new dataset. We do not foresee harms specific to this work beyond those of robot learning in general.

Joint action and future-feature prediction improves LIBERO-Plus success over action-only training for each of three training seeds, raising mean success from 74.35% to 76.47%, a gain of 2.12 points (Table 7 ). Figure 3 A shows this mean gain; its in-distribution bar uses the seed-42 pair at 150k updates, evaluated on 2,000 LIBERO episodes. Both objectives train on all 1,743 LIBERO episodes of the original pipeline for 150,000 updates with image augmentation and encoder LoRA, whereas the headline policies use the revised pipeline (Appendix B ), so these controls are not directly comparable to Table 1 . The action-only control omits future-feature supervision and computation while preserving the action pathway. For each objective and training seed, we select the checkpoint with the highest LIBERO success from the 30k, 60k, 90k, 120k, and 150k grid and evaluate it on all 10,030 LIBERO-Plus episodes with EMA weights, action-noise scale 1 redrawn at every replan, ten denoising steps, and ten-action execution chunks. Selection picks the same step for both objectives within each seed. Paired tests use identical task and evaluation-seed episodes for the two objectives.

On 5,000 episodes per regime, each policy on its own set of evaluation episodes, joint training achieves 80.16% clean and 39.02% randomized success, against 73.14% and 35.34% for action-only training. Both policies use the final augmentation recipe (Table 10 ), all 2,500 clean demonstrations, 150,000 training updates, and a global batch of 400, split into four data-parallel ranks of 100 for joint training and eight of 50 for action-only training; the action-only policy neither loads nor computes future targets. Block B compares frozen, static V-JEPA 2.1 features with Wan2.2 VAE latents at 150k updates, with action and future-feature prediction on the 95% split. Within each benchmark, feature dimensions, normalization, and input and output projections remain representation-specific, so the comparison concerns the two representation systems rather than their pretraining objectives in isolation. On RoboTwin, both policies use 384-dimensional, 12-layer transformers with patch grouping for observations and future targets and are evaluated on 5,000-episode clean and randomized manifests with 24-action execution chunks. On LIBERO, both use the 768-dimensional, 12-layer B transformer with 2 × 2\times spatial mean pooling and 10-action execution chunks; LIBERO evaluation instead uses a 600-step budget per suite and 30 settling steps, and LIBERO-Plus evaluation uses action-noise scale 1. On LIBERO-Plus, V-JEPA succeeds in 5,773 episodes and Wan2.2 in 5,173. All evaluations use EMA weights, a single observation context, and 10 denoising steps.

Two further RoboTwin comparisons pool the future targets, each evaluated on 5,000 episodes per regime (clean only for the first). With full-data, static-feature training and patch-grouped observations, V-JEPA and Wan2.2 achieve 61.50% and 61.44% clean success at 150k. In the second, with 768-dimensional transformers, Wan2.2 leads on clean success (63.90% versus 61.12%), whereas V-JEPA leads on randomized success (15.00% versus 1.28%). V-JEPA’s advantage therefore holds in randomized scenes but not consistently in clean ones.

Block C compares three frozen-encoder policies with patch grouping, trained on the 95% split, that differ only in the encoding: static, tube, or tube-motion. Each regime uses 1,000 episodes on the same scenes, and randomized success is read at the checkpoint selected on clean episodes: 150k for static and tube-motion, and 120k for tube.

On RoboTwin, grouping neighboring features into one token by concatenation (patch grouping) instead of averaging them (mean pooling) changes clean success by + 0.3 +0.3 points and raises randomized success by 4.1 points. Both policies apply the reduction to two-frame observations and to motion-based future targets and are compared at 150k updates; each clean and randomized evaluation uses 1,000 episodes, 32 samples per pixel, rendering depth 8, OIDN denoising, and action noise fixed within each episode. The pooling policy uses the full training set and the patch-grouping policy the 95% split, and their target normalization and projections also differ, so the comparison does not isolate the reduction operator. By contrast, on LIBERO, in a one-variable comparison between stored-feature S policies with tube-motion encoding at 150k updates, evaluated identically on 2,000 episodes, mean pooling reaches 94.05% against 89.35% for patch grouping. The final recipe uses patch grouping on RoboTwin, reducing the head camera 2 × 2\times and the wrist cameras 4 × 4\times , and 2 × 2\times mean pooling on LIBERO (Appendix B ). Appendix E.3 reports a related sweep that pools only the future targets.

These studies target robustness to changes in the observations through camera and proprioception dropout, image augmentation, and encoder adaptation (Section 4.2 ). All LIBERO variants in blocks D and F train on the 95% split and are selected on LIBERO success: stored-feature policies with a frozen encoder at 90k updates, and online-encoder variants at 120k.

Before training, we encode every demonstration once with the frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder and store the resulting features. Stored-feature policies, used in most design studies, read both observations and future targets from these stores and never run the encoder during training. Encoder LoRA and image augmentation require encoding the observations at every training step, so the final policies encode their observation clips online but still read their future targets from the stores. Encoding the targets online as well would dominate the encoder cost of each step, since each camera’s targets span 16 frames, eight times as many encoder tokens as its two-frame observation clip. Targets from the adapting encoder also do not improve success (Appendix E.1 ), so the targets remain those of the frozen encoder.

The features are then reduced spatially before entering the World DiT. Mean pooling, the simplest reduction, averages each 2 × 2 2\times 2 neighborhood of a feature grid into one token. Because it can be applied once when the features are precomputed, it shrinks the stored features fourfold. Most of our development therefore used pre-pooled stores, which are much smaller and far easier to load during training than full-resolution V-JEPA features. Patch grouping instead concatenates neighboring features into one wider token, reducing the number of tokens without discarding any feature values, but the stored features keep their full size. Mean pooling suffices on LIBERO, whereas on RoboTwin the detail it averages away matters: patch grouping raises randomized success by 4.1 points (Appendix A.1 ), so the final RoboTwin recipe uses patch grouping.

On LIBERO, all three sizes train on all 1,777 demonstrations retained by the revised pipeline (Appendix B ) for 150,000 updates, and we report the final checkpoints’ performances averaged over three training seeds; L additionally uses full-depth LoRA. The final RoboTwin S, B, and L policies train on the 2,438 clean demonstrations retained by the revised pipeline (Appendix B ) with three training seeds each. For each seed, the checkpoint is selected among 90k, 120k, and 150k updates on a 1,000-episode clean grid disjoint from the evaluation episodes, which picks 150k for every seed except one L seed (120k); the selected policies are evaluated on 5,000 episodes per condition with action noise redrawn at every replan, and we report the mean over seeds.

LIBERO scores are success rates over the four standard suites. LIBERO-Plus scores are success rates over all 10,030 evaluation episodes of the seven perturbation categories, including background textures, weighting every episode rather than every category equally. Literature aggregates are recomputed from reported per-category rates when needed. JEPA-WAM trains only on these 20 tasks, whereas our policies train on all 50. The subset is easier than the full benchmark: per-task DP3 and ACT policies reach 73.9% and 51.8% clean success on it ( Lin et al., 2026 ) , against 55.2% and 29.7% over all 50 tasks ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . Projected to all 50 tasks, JEPA-WAM’s success is estimated at 65.5% clean and 25.0% randomized (see the full-suite estimate below), below every La-JEPA size in Table 2 . Table 13 compares the instruction a policy receives under four sources. The LIBERO training demonstrations store each task’s instruction in their metadata, identical to the instruction that standard LIBERO evaluation derives from the task’s file name. The released LIBERO-Plus evaluator derives the instruction from the variant’s file name instead, so every non-language variant receives the training instruction followed by the perturbation’s parameters. Flex- π \pi ( Yan et al., 2026a ) replaces it with the :language annotation of the variant’s BDDL file, falling back to the base task’s file for camera, robot-initial-state, and sensor-noise variants. These annotations are written independently of the training instructions: across the 8,493 non-language variants, only 2,351 match the training instruction exactly and 3,148 up to capitalization, so most variants still receive a paraphrase that the policy never saw during training. Our corrected text gives every non-language variant its base task’s training instruction verbatim. For the 1,537 language variants, whose paraphrases are the intended perturbation, the released and corrected texts are identical, and Flex- π \pi ’s annotations contain the same words but differ in capitalization for 1,209 of them. All re-evaluations share one protocol; NowWAM, Fast-WAM, and ImageWAM, whose released evaluations use longer step limits, are scored at the upstream per-suite limits like every other policy. Table 14 reports both evaluations. Because the corruption affects policies to different degrees, released-instruction scores partly rank policies by their sensitivity to corrupted text rather than by their robustness to the intended perturbation: correcting the instructions reverses the order of NowWAM and La-JEPA B and L, and of Cosmos Policy and La-JEPA S. With corrected instructions, S is on par with NowWAM, and L’s 1.8-point lead exceeds both its seed-to-seed standard deviation (0.3 points) and the binomial standard error of a single 10,030-episode evaluation (about 0.35 points).

Tables 15 and 5 time complete benchmark policy calls, not executed actions or control-loop cycles. Each timed call includes fresh instruction tokenization and encoding, input preparation, transfer, and host-side action output; loading, compilation, simulation, and transport are excluded. Text and vision encoders run on parallel streams where supported. Eager execution is uncompiled; original-kernel CUDA graphs reduce launch overhead without changing kernels; optimized builds also compile the computation. The head-to-head WAM rows use ten denoising steps and 32 predicted actions, whereas the three-step rows and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} (official JAX JIT, ten steps, native ten-action horizon) are separate operating points. Each method keeps its native inputs: La-JEPA uses two 256 × 256 256\times 256 cameras with two adjacent frames and FLAN-T5-large, timed in FP32 (our success evaluations use FP16), whereas in our setup Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM use two 224 × 224 224\times 224 single-frame cameras and BF16 UMT5-XXL ( Chung et al., 2023 ) . Action noise is pre-drawn and copied inside the timed call for La-JEPA, and drawn on the CPU inside the call for Fast-WAM. LingBot-VA is timed on the same device under the same protocol with its native implementation and appears, rounded to 10 ms, only in Table 5 .

For La-JEPA, original-kernel CUDA graphs reproduce eager actions bit-for-bit across 36 replays per model on 12 inputs that vary observations, instructions, and noise. Compilation is not bit-exact: the maximum ten-step action differences are 0.010, 0.021, and 0.009 for S, B, and L. Our simulation success rates use uncompiled execution, which the CUDA graphs reproduce exactly, whereas the physical-robot La-JEPA policy runs compiled. For Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM, original-kernel graphs exceed the available GPU memory in our implementation.

Using the original-pipeline checkpoints (Appendix B ), we evaluate the exact timed builds on 2,000 LIBERO episodes with a 700-step budget in every suite (Appendix B ), with action noise of scale 1 redrawn at every replan, and compare each with uncompiled execution of the same checkpoint using paired McNemar tests. Compiled ten-step builds reach 95.20%, 97.05%, and 96.25% for S, B, and L, against 94.30%, 97.35%, and 96.50% uncompiled ( p = 0.15 p=0.15 , 0.59 0.59 , and 0.69 0.69 ). In separate evaluation runs, ten-step CUDA-graph builds reach 94.70%, 97.00%, and 96.35% ( p = 0.55 p=0.55 , 0.50 0.50 , and 0.84 0.84 ), and the three-step B graph build 96.90% against 97.30% ( p = 0.45 p=0.45 ). None of the seven paired comparisons differs significantly. The timed L build applies LoRA to the final eight encoder blocks and is selected at 150k updates.

With serial rather than parallel text and vision encoding, optimized ten-step calls take 19, 26, and 61 ms for S, B, and L, against 92 ms for Fast-WAM and 54 ms for Faster-WAM, leaving the speedups essentially unchanged.

This appendix describes the physical platform, the four tasks, demonstration collection, and the training and evaluation protocol behind Table 5 , and reports completion times.

A tabletop Franka Panda with a parallel gripper uses a wrist-mounted RealSense D405 camera and a fixed external RealSense D435 camera. A GPU workstation runs Linux with a real-time kernel. Policies receive both camera views, proprioception, and a task instruction, and execute end-effector deltas and gripper commands through Polymetis 2 2 2 https://facebookresearch.github.io/fairo/polymetis/ and the Franka Control Interface.

Cube placement uses a red wooden cube and a bowl. Fruit picking requires removing a bamboo steamer’s lid, setting it down, and then picking the correct fruit, a plum, from inside the steamer. Push T requires pushing a wooden T onto a T shape marked on the table. Dish manipulation requires placing both plates, then the spoon on the gray plate and the fork on the pink plate, in one uninterrupted rollout; plate locations are fixed, but the utensils’ starting positions are interchangeable. Every training demonstration and evaluation rollout contains the complete uninterrupted sequence of its task. Figure 5 shows the initial scene of each task from the external camera.

SpaceMouse teleoperation provides six-degree-of-freedom end-effector control through the same interface. We record camera observations, robot state, end-effector pose, and gripper state at 10 Hz, collecting 100 demonstrations per task (400 in total). Initial cube positions vary within 10 ​ cm × 10 ​ cm 10\,\mathrm{cm}\times 10\,\mathrm{cm} , and plum positions vary within the steamer; Push T and dish manipulation use smaller placement variations, including utensil rearrangements.

Policies train jointly on the four language-conditioned tasks using their respective recipes. Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM train for 30 epochs; La-JEPA trains its B policy transformer from scratch with encoder LoRA but without image augmentation. Table 5 reports counts over 20 rollouts per task, with explicit ten-rollout denominators for LingBot-VA’s dish result. Utensil 1 and Utensil 2 denote successful placement of the first and second utensils on plates, irrespective of utensil identity or order. Position additionally requires the correct spoon–gray and fork–pink assignments and success at all preceding stages; the two plate stages share one table column because their counts are identical. Average weights the four tasks equally, using Position for dish, in mean successes out of 20; LingBot-VA’s average is omitted because its dish result uses 10 trials rather than 20.

Table 17 reports the mean and standard deviation of completion time over successful trials. La-JEPA is the fastest policy without embodied pretraining on every task and the fastest overall on fruit picking and Push T, while π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} is fastest on cube placement and dish manipulation. Our main hypothesis for LingBot-VA’s low Push T and dish success is that it requires substantially more real-robot finetuning than the other policies; independently of success, its completion times, three to eleven times longer than those of the other policies, make it impractical for closed-loop control on this platform. Its dish entry comes from its single successful trial.

This appendix collects results that inform but do not define the final recipe: adapted future targets, evaluation-time settings, future-only pooling, representation diagnostics, and per-task RoboTwin success.

On LIBERO with L, we replace the frozen future targets with targets from an EMA of the adapting encoder, keeping the clips, observation processing, and normalization statistics of the frozen-target policy and passing no gradients through the target path. The adapted-target policy, selected at 90k updates, achieves 81.65% on LIBERO-Plus, against 82.26% for the frozen-target policy at 120k, both trained with the original pipeline (Appendix B ) and at action-noise scale 1. Adapted targets do not improve success (paired McNemar p = 0.096 p=0.096 ), so the final recipe retains frozen targets.

At the 120k checkpoints of the original-pipeline policies (Appendix B ), we vary the execution chunk length, the number of denoising steps, and the action-noise scale for L and B, and test three-step inference for S (Table 19 ); the reference executes ten actions per replan with ten denoising steps and noise scale 1, and LIBERO runs use a 700-step budget in every suite (Appendix B ). Executing only five actions reduces LIBERO-Plus success by 3.29 points for L and 3.45 for B, whereas the number of denoising steps matters less: with three steps, B and L stay within one point of their ten-step references on both benchmarks, and S obtains 94.50% against 94.30% on LIBERO ( p = 0.81 p=0.81 , paired McNemar). Three-step calls take 23 ms for B and 39 ms for L with original-kernel CUDA graphs (Table 15 ), an operating point separate from the ten-step latency comparison. No tested noise scale gives a statistically supported aggregate improvement in the paired comparisons; the original L policy reaches 82.26% at the default scale 1 (Appendix B ), and the best single scale, 0.5, reaches 82.50%.
